weak: If you build something that hurts people then it is your fault. Being careful is not an excuse, because the people who got hurt are still hurt, and someone has to pay for it.
Companies always say they were careful after something goes wrong. We cannot check that, so we should just blame them according to the damage, otherwise they will never take responsibility.
Nobody can predict everything an AI will do. It would be unfair to blame engineers for things they could not have known, so they should not be blamed at all if they followed the rules.
The law already decides this with liability and insurance, so there is no point in a philosophical debate about blame. The courts will sort it out case by case like they always do.
AI is too complicated for anyone to fully understand, including the people who build it. So really nobody is to blame when it goes wrong, it is just a risk we accept by using new technology.

positions: Blame attaches to judgement, not to fortune, so a builder who judged well and was unlucky is blameless whatever the damage.
I reject the motion. The harm a system does depends on fortune; the builder's judgement does not, and only judgement can deserve blame.
A Stoic must deny that blame scales with harm. Careful builders who assented only to what the evidence supported acted well, whatever followed.
The motion makes blame depend on outcomes, which are never up to anyone. Blame belongs only to what was up to the builders: how carefully they judged.
reasons: Epictetus is clear that outcomes are not up to us; only our judgements and choices are. Two equally careful teams can deploy equally well-tested systems and one can cause a disaster through no difference in their conduct. Blaming that team more is blaming them for fortune.

The Stoics compared the wise person to an archer. The archer is responsible for drawing and aiming well; once the arrow leaves the bow, the wind is not hers. A builder who tested, audited and deployed with care has aimed well, and the gust that followed is not her fault.

Blame is a judgement about a faculty that went wrong. If the builders' judgement did not go wrong, there is nothing to blame, however terrible the result. To scale blame by harm is to blame the world for being the way it is and pin it on a person.

None of this makes the harm unimportant. The builders should help repair it and learn from it, because that is what a rational and social being does. But helping repair is not the same as being to blame, and running the two together corrupts both.
examples: Two teams ship the same carefully audited model. One is deployed in a quiet market and one in a hospital where a rare error kills a patient. Their conduct was identical.
A doctor who follows the best evidence and loses a patient to a reaction nobody could have predicted is not a worse doctor than her lucky colleague.
A ship's captain who navigated well and still lost cargo to a storm is not blamed for the storm, though he may grieve the loss.

objections.claim: a good person carries the weight of harm they caused even when blameless, and a builder who calmly says it was only fortune reveals a defect of character.
objections.answer: Carrying the weight and being to blame are different. The Stoic builder can grieve, repair and resolve to do better without accepting blame for what was never up to her. Calm is not indifference; it is clarity about what she controlled.
objections.why: The argument never says what the careful builder should feel or do after the harm, so it reads as indifference to the victims.

objections.claim: blame is a tool for changing future behaviour, and its value depends on what it achieves, not on whether the builder's judgement was correct.
objections.answer: Using blame as a tool on people who judged well teaches them nothing, because there was nothing in their judgement to correct. Blame aimed at fortune is not a tool for improvement but a way of feeling that someone paid.
objections.why: It does not consider whether blaming careful builders might still make future builders more careful.

positions: Blame is a tool for changing future behaviour, so it should track what would have prevented the harm, and punishing care that failed by chance prevents nothing.
I reject the motion. Blame proportional to harm punishes careful builders for bad luck and gives everyone the wrong incentives.
A utilitarian should oppose this motion, because blame is justified by its effects, and blaming careful people in proportion to harm produces worse effects than the alternatives.
The motion gets blame backwards. We should blame in whatever way best prevents future harm, and that means rewarding care, not punishing it when luck runs out.
reasons: Blame, punishment and praise are practices, and practices are justified by their consequences. Their job is to make people more careful in future. Blaming a team that did everything right teaches the industry that care does not protect you, which weakens the incentive to take care at all.

If blame scaled with harm regardless of care, the rational response for builders would be to avoid high-stakes uses altogether. That would withdraw useful systems from medicine and transport, where the expected benefits are large, and make people worse off overall.

There are better tools for the harm itself. Compensation schemes and insurance can make victims whole without pretending the builders were at fault. Separating compensation from blame lets us help the injured and keep the incentives right at the same time.

What should be blamed is what could have been done better: skipped tests, ignored warnings, rushed releases. Tracking those failures directly gives builders a clear reason to avoid them, while blame by outcome gives them a lottery.
examples: If an audited diagnostic model makes one fatal error in a million cases, blaming its builders fully might stop the next team building a model that saves thousands.
Vaccine makers are shielded by compensation schemes because blaming them for rare reactions would make vaccines scarcer, and far more people would die.
A pilot who followed every procedure in a freak storm is not grounded for life, because that would teach other pilots nothing useful.

objections.claim: treating blame as a pure incentive misses that a good person acknowledges harm they caused, and a culture that only manages incentives breeds builders who shrug.
objections.answer: Acknowledging harm can itself be encouraged, and it should be, because it helps victims and keeps builders attentive. But acknowledgement is not proportional blame, and confusing the two would make the practice worse at preventing the next harm.
objections.why: It does not answer whether builders who see blame purely as an incentive would come to care less about the people harmed.

objections.claim: blame belongs to faulty judgement and nothing else, so its usefulness is irrelevant: a careful builder is blameless whether or not blaming her would deter anyone.
objections.answer: In ordinary cases the two views agree, since faulty judgement is what we want to deter. Where they come apart, the question is what the practice of blame is for, and a practice that helps nobody has no claim on us.
objections.why: The argument never says whether it would be right to blame a careful builder if doing so happened to deter others.

positions: A good person carries the weight of harm they caused even when blameless, so proportional blame is mistaken, while a builder who shrugs reveals a defect of character.
I reject the motion as stated, because blame tracks fault, but I reject the careless alternative too: the builders still owe the harm something blame cannot measure.
The motion confuses blame with what Williams called agent-regret. Careful builders are not to blame in proportion to harm, but they cannot treat the harm as nothing to do with them.
Proportional blame is wrong, yet so is a clean conscience. A virtuous builder feels the weight of what their system did, and that feeling is part of being good.
reasons: Bernard Williams described a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, kills a child. He is not to blame, yet we would think less of him if he felt nothing more than a bystander. That feeling, agent-regret, attaches to what you did, not to what you did wrong.

Blame tracks fault, and the careful builders were not at fault, so the motion is false. But virtue is not just avoiding fault. A good person responds to having caused harm with grief, a wish to repair it, and changed attention, and those responses are owed even here.

Aristotle thought the right feeling at the right time towards the right people is part of virtue. The right feeling for a builder whose system killed someone is not guilt, which would be false, but neither is it the calm of someone who checked the boxes. The calm is the defect.

Character shows in how we carry what we did not intend. A team that says it followed procedure and moves on teaches its juniors that the procedure is the whole of responsibility. A team that sits with the harm teaches them that people, not procedures, are what they answer to.
examples: Imagine an engineer who learns her model contributed to a death and says only that the audit was passed. Nothing she said is false, and something is still badly wrong.
A driver who hits a child who ran into the road is not prosecuted, but we expect him to visit the family, and we think less of him if he does not.
A surgeon who loses a patient despite perfect technique does not blame herself, but she does not go to lunch as if nothing happened.

objections.claim: if the builders are not to blame then their feelings are their own business, and what matters is compensating victims and preventing future harm.
objections.answer: Feelings are not private ornaments; they shape what people attend to. Builders who feel the weight of past harm look harder for the next one, and an institution that treats regret as irrelevant gradually stops noticing who it hurts.
objections.why: It never says what the victims gain from the builders' regret, which is the utilitarian's whole question.

objections.claim: fortune is not up to the builders, so any weight they carry for it is a false judgement that something bad happened to them, and the wise builder would set it down.
objections.answer: The Stoic is right that guilt here would be false, but wrong that every response to unintended harm is a mistake. Agent-regret is not a false belief about fault; it is an accurate recognition that this harm came through my hands.
objections.why: The argument does not explain why a feeling that matches no fault is anything other than a misjudgement.

positions: A builder's blame is measured by what the position of builder owed the people the system serves, so a careful builder who met those duties is not to blame in proportion to the harm.
I reject the motion. One is to blame for failing what one's role requires, not for the size of what went wrong, though the role still requires an account and repair.
The motion misnames the duty. A builder is not answerable for the harm as such but for whether they did what the position of builder requires towards the people who rely on the system.
To blame in proportion to harm is wrong, but so is walking away. The careful builder owes the injured an account and a share in repairing things, because that is part of the role too.
reasons: What you owe attaches to a position, not to the world at large. A builder owes the people their system touches care in making it, honesty about its limits, and an answer when it fails. A builder who did all of that has done what the position requires.

Getting names right matters. To call a careful builder culpable in proportion to the harm is to use blame for something that is not fault, and once the word means that, it no longer distinguishes the builders who cut corners from those who did not.

Roles carry duties after the fact as well as before. The relationship between builder and user does not end at the release, so a careful builder whose system harmed someone still owes them acknowledgement, an explanation, and help in making it right.

Humaneness is shown in how one responds to those one's work has affected. A builder who points only to the audit has misunderstood the relationship; one who meets the injured, explains and repairs is being what a builder should be.
examples: A team that tested its model carefully learns it misread one group's medical scans. They are not culpable, but they contact the clinics, explain what happened, and fund the follow-up scans.
An apprentice builder follows every check her master taught and still a joint fails. The master does not blame her, but both go to the house to make it good.
A firm's lawyer says the careful team has no liability. The team's lead visits the family anyway, because whatever the law says, they are the people who built it.

objections.claim: talk of what the role requires is beside the point, because blame exists to change future behaviour and should be assigned wherever it prevents the most harm.
objections.answer: Blame used only as a lever stops tracking what anyone did, and people who cannot see why they are blamed stop trusting the roles that hold them together. The role tells you what to change; blaming the careful does not.
objections.why: It sets out what the builder owes without saying whether assigning blame that way would make systems any safer.

objections.claim: the Confucian measures the builder's duty from inside the role, when the people harmed were never asked what the builders owed them in the first place.
objections.answer: That is a real gap in letting roles define duties: the people on the other end of a role may never have agreed to its terms. The answer is that a role's duties include listening to those it serves, and a builder who never asked has not met them.
objections.why: It defines the builder's duty by the role without asking who set the role's terms or whether the injured had any part in them.

positions: The harm is a broken relationship between the builders and the people it fell on, so what is owed is not blame sized to the damage but the builders' part in mending that relationship.
I reject the motion. Blame in proportion to harm treats the matter as a debt to be calculated; what the harm calls for is repair between people.

Proportional blame misreads the situation. When a system harms people, the relationships between builders, users and community are damaged, and careful or not, the builders are part of restoring them.
The motion asks the wrong question. Whether the builders were careful affects whether they are at fault, but every builder whose system harmed people owes them a share in making things whole.
reasons: A harm reads as a failure of relationship, not only a bad outcome. Scaling blame to the damage treats the injured as a quantity of loss; bringing builders and injured together to repair what was broken treats them as people still bound up with one another.

People become who they are through one another, and that includes the builders. A team that cannot face the people its work harmed loses part of its own standing among them, which is why repair is something builders need as well as owe.

Care matters to fault, because taking care is itself a way of honouring the people a system will reach. Builders who did what could reasonably be done for those people stood in the right relation to them, and blaming them as careless builders are blamed treats that relation as worth nothing.

The question of who was left out of deciding applies here too. If the people later harmed had no say in how the system was built or tested, the builders owe them not just repair but a place in deciding what changes now.
examples: A lending model wrongly flags a neighbourhood's applicants. The careful builders meet residents, listen, and rebuild the model with their input rather than paying a fine and moving on.
A careful team's translation tool mistranslates a medical instruction. They go to the clinic that was hurt by it and work through the fix with the staff who saw the harm.
A town's water-monitoring model misses a contamination. The builders join the town meeting, hear what it cost people, and help set up checks the residents trust.

objections.claim: blame attaches to judgement, not to fortune, so the careful builder who judged well owes nothing, and talk of repairing relationships confuses misfortune with wrongdoing.
objections.answer: Owing repair is not the same as being at fault. The builders' judgement may have been sound and they may be blameless, yet the relationship between them and the people harmed is still damaged, and mending it is still theirs to help with.
objections.why: It asks for repair without explaining why blameless builders owe anything at all.

objections.claim: compensation paid to those harmed does measurable good, while talk of restoring relationships promises something nobody can count or check.
objections.answer: Compensation can be counted, and it should be paid. But whether the people harmed are restored can be checked too, by asking them whether the builders met them, explained what went wrong and changed what they do. Money paid without that leaves the relationship as broken as before.
objections.why: It speaks of restoring relationships without saying what the restoring adds to compensation, or whether the injured want it.

positions: Volition weighs as much as what follows, so builders who acted with care and good intention are not to blame in proportion to the harm, though they stay bound to keep examining the system.
I reject the motion. Blame follows intention as well as outcome, and careful builders acting to reduce harm are not culpable for what they could not foresee.
Proportional blame ignores intention, which is half of what makes an act what it is, but a good intention does not end the builders' duty to find and stop the harm.
A Buddhist Ethicist rejects the motion, with a warning: care and good intention lessen blame, yet they never excuse a builder from looking hard at what their system goes on doing.
reasons: An act is weighed by the volition behind it as much as by what follows. Builders who intended to help, and took real care, acted from a sound intention, and blaming them as if they had acted carelessly ignores half of what their act was.

Good intention cannot be a blanket excuse. A well-meaning builder who stops checking once the system ships is not acting from care any longer, and the damage that follows is theirs in a way the first unforeseen harm was not.

The discourse to Rahula asks that an act be examined after it is done, and if it is found to harm oneself or another, that it be acknowledged and not repeated. That is the builders' duty here: to admit the harm and change what caused it.

What happened arose from many conditions: the data, the users, the setting, the builders' choices. Blame in proportion to harm treats the builders as the single cause, when compassion asks for an honest account of all the conditions and of their part among them.
examples: A team's careful chatbot gives harmful advice to a user in crisis. They are not culpable for an unforeseeable failure, but they publish what happened and retrain it within the week.
A careful builder's model denies a loan it should have granted. She is not blamed, yet she spends the next month reviewing every similar refusal for the same mistake.
A well-meaning startup's tool harms users and the founders point to their good intentions. Their intention was sound at launch; their refusal to look again is not.

objections.claim: intention is invisible and irrelevant to the people harmed, so blame should track what deters future harm, not the builders' inner states.
objections.answer: Intention is not invisible in practice: it shows in how carefully builders tested and how fast they respond. And a rule that blames the careful as much as the careless removes the reason to be careful at all.
objections.why: It weighs the builders' intention heavily and never says what that does for the people who were harmed.

objections.claim: the builders owe the people their system serves an account and repair because of the relationship they stand in, whatever their intentions were.
objections.answer: That is right, and it is what examining the act afterwards requires: acknowledging the harm to those it fell on and working to undo it. Good intention lessens blame; it does not lessen what is owed to the injured.
objections.why: It treats intention as settling the matter and never says what the builders owe the particular people who were hurt.
